why.support: You follow steps every day. Sometimes you teach someone else. If they can follow your steps without help, you nailed it.
why.core: At work and at home you'll follow instructions every day, and sometimes you'll be the one teaching. If someone can follow your steps without asking you a single question, you've nailed it.
why.extend: Instructions are everywhere at work: safety procedures, recipes, closing the till. Writing them well means thinking like your reader — what they know, and what they'll get wrong.

articles.title: What makes instructions work

body.support:
Instructions have one job. Help someone do it right, the first time.

Good instructions have:

1. **A title.** *How to make a cheese toastie.*
2. **What you need.** A list of things to get first.
3. **Steps with numbers.** In order. One action in each step.
4. **A doing word first.** *Cut. Spread. Press.*
5. **Exact words.** *Two slices*, not *some bread*.
6. **Pictures and warnings.** *Careful: hot!*

The secret? **Test it.** Give your steps to someone. Watch. Don't help. If they get stuck, fix that step.
body.core:
Instructions are a **text type** with one job: help someone do something right, the first time. Good ones share the same features.

1. **A clear title.** Say what you'll make or do: *How to make a cheese toastie*.
2. **What you need.** List the materials and tools before the steps, so nobody gets halfway and stops.
3. **Numbered steps in order.** One action per step. If the order matters (and it usually does), the numbers show it.
4. **Start with a doing word.** *Cut*, *spread*, *press*, *wait*. It tells the reader exactly what to do.
5. **Be precise.** *Two slices* beats *some bread*. *For 3 minutes* beats *for a bit*.
6. **Pictures and warnings.** A photo or diagram can save a hundred words. A warning (*Careful: hot!*) keeps people safe.

The secret? **Test it.** Give your instructions to someone who has never done the task. Watch, and don't help. Every time they get stuck, you've found a step to fix.
body.extend:
Instructions (or procedures) are a **text type** designed for one purpose: to get a reader to complete a task correctly, first time, without help. Effective instructions share recognisable features.

1. **A specific title** that names the outcome: *How to make a cheese toastie*.
2. **Materials and equipment** listed up front, so the reader can prepare.
3. **Numbered, sequential steps**, each containing a single action.
4. **Imperative verbs** (commands) at the start of each step: *cut*, *spread*, *press*.
5. **Precise language**: quantities, times and positions, so nothing is left to guess.
6. **Visuals and warnings**, which often communicate faster and more safely than words.

Writers rarely get instructions right in one go, because they know the task too well and skip “obvious” steps. That's why professionals **test** them on real users: watch silently, note every hesitation, and revise.

caseStudies.title: The Exact Instructions Challenge

body.support:
In 2017, a YouTuber called **Josh Darnit** made a video. It went viral.

His two kids wrote steps for making a **peanut butter and jam sandwich**. Josh did **exactly** what the words said. Nothing more.

It went badly. The steps said to put peanut butter on the bread. So he put the whole jar on the bread!

The kids rewrote their steps again and again.

It is funny. But it shows something real. When you know a task well, you skip steps. Your reader can't read your mind.
body.core:
In 2017, a YouTuber called **Josh Darnit** posted a video that went viral. His two kids had to write instructions for making a **peanut butter and jam sandwich**. Josh would then follow them **exactly** — doing only what the words said.

It went badly. When the instructions said to put peanut butter on the bread, he put the whole jar on the bread. When they said to spread it, he used his hand. The kids rewrote their instructions again and again, getting more and more frustrated.

It looks like a joke, but teachers around the world use the same challenge. It shows something real: you know a task so well that you skip steps. Your reader can't read your mind.
body.extend:
In 2017, YouTuber **Josh Darnit** posted a video that spread fast online. His two children wrote instructions for making a **peanut butter and jam sandwich**. He then followed them exactly, doing only what the words said.

The results were chaos. “Put peanut butter on the bread” got the whole jar placed on a slice. “Spread it” was done with his hand. The kids rewrote their steps again and again, and got more and more frustrated.

The “exact instructions” challenge is now a common classroom activity. It shows a real problem in writing for an audience. When you know a task well, you skip steps that seem obvious to you. They are not obvious to your reader.

source.name: Scary Mommy — “Josh Darnit’s peanut butter and jelly video”; KTAR News (11 February 2017)

teacher.overview: Students learn the structures and features of instructional texts (title, materials, numbered steps, imperative verbs, precise detail, warnings), then plan, draft and edit a how-to for something they can do. The hands-on test drive has a partner follow it literally while the writer watches, then revise. The case study is the viral “Exact Instructions Challenge”.
prep: Optional: show the Exact Instructions Challenge video (preview first; it's on YouTube).
Gather simple materials for test drives (paper for folding, Lego, bread and spreads if your school allows food), or let students act tasks out.
Have a real manual or recipe for comparison.

teacher.answers:
**How-to:** 1 you need (materials); 2 doing word + exact time; 3 one action per step; 4 precise detail (butter side out); 5 warning; 6 how you know it's done (until golden).

**Clear or not clear?** Put the bread in — not clear (Put 2 slices of bread in the toaster). Press the green button on the left — clear. Wait a bit — not clear (Wait 2 minutes). Do the rest like normal — not clear. Fold the paper in half… — clear. Add some water… — not clear (split into steps with amounts).

**Case study rewrite (sample):** Use a knife to scoop a spoonful of peanut butter, then spread it evenly over one side of one slice.
